metric_rationale: This metric is the proportion of trials on which subjects choose TAKE-THE-BEST's favored option, restricted to the 'pure conflict' trials where the two heuristics disagree (the tally majority favors the opposite option to the top discriminating cue). In this design those are trials T2,T3,T4,T6,T7,T8,T10,T12,T15,T16 — 10 of 16 trial types, i.e. 60 of the 96 trials per subject, so the per-subject estimate is based on a large sample and is very stable. Predicted values: under TTB, every conflict trial has identical choice probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 > 0.5 for any beta>0, eps<0.5 (e.g. ~0.73 at beta=1, ~0.87 averaged over the parameter prior, approaching 1 at large beta). Under Tallying, the same trials have probability (1-eps)*sigmoid(-m*beta)+eps/2 with tally margins against the TTB option of 1, 2, or 3, which is strictly BELOW 0.5 for any beta>0 (e.g. ~0.17 at beta=1, ~0.13 averaged over the prior, approaching 0 at large beta). So the two theories sit on opposite sides of 0.5 with a large signed gap (~0.5-0.75) that persists across the whole plausible parameter range, while per-subject binomial variance is tiny (sd ~0.06-0.12 per subject with 60 conflict trials). I deliberately excluded tie trials (where Tallying guesses at exactly 0.5) and agreement trials, because including them only dilutes the mean gap without reducing variance enough to compensate. The metric is a simple proportion, so it is well-defined both on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's slice, and it involves no free parameters, no fitting, and no hashing of the list-valued rating columns.

The design's 16 trial types split into 4 agree types (tally winner = TTB winner: trials 1, 3, 5, 7) and 12 conflict types (tally winner = TTB loser: trials 2, 4, 6, 8-16). The metric is the difference between overall choice-consistency with Tallying and overall choice-consistency with TTB. On agree trials the two consistencies are identical and cancel; on conflict trials they are exact complements, so the metric equals 0.75 * (2*P(choose tally winner | conflict trials) - 1). Under simulated Tallying data, P(tally winner | conflict) = softmax over tallies (e.g. ~0.77 at beta=1, ~1.0 at large beta), giving a strongly POSITIVE value (~+0.4 at beta=1, up to +0.75). Under simulated TTB data, P(tally winner | conflict) = 1 - sigmoid(beta) (TTB always follows the top cue regardless of how many cues oppose it, including the 1-vs-5 anchors), giving a strongly NEGATIVE value (~-0.35 at beta=1, down to -0.75). The between-theory gap in the mean is therefore large at every plausible parameter setting (roughly 0.09 even at beta=0.1, ~0.27 at beta=0.3, ~0.75 at beta>=2), while per-subject variance stays tight because each subject contributes 96 trials (72 conflict) of simple binary indicators: per-subject SD ~0.08, so with N=25 subjects the Welch t-statistic ranges from ~4 (worst case, near-random parameters) to ~35 (moderate/large beta), comfortably below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on any single subject's slice (it is just a difference of two proportions), and it is side-balanced (the tally winner is option A on exactly 8 of the 16 trial types), so position/label bias cancels in expectation.

The metric is the partial OLS coefficient of the validity-weighted evidence difference d = sum(v over A-won cues) - sum(v over B-won cues) in a regression of the chose-A indicator on [intercept, signed tally margin, d], pooled over all trials.

WHY IT IS EXACTLY ZERO UNDER TALLYING (for every beta, epsilon): Tallying's P(A) = sigmoid(beta*(a_wins - b_wins)) (plus a symmetric lapse), i.e., a function of the signed margin m alone. The design's trial set is perfectly mirrored within every margin level: the d-values of all trials sharing a given margin sum to exactly zero (margin 0: +0.55,+0.40,+0.15,0,+0.05,-0.55,-0.40,-0.15,0,-0.05; margin +1: +1.30...+0.20 with the exact negatives in margin -1; margin +2: +1.90,+1.05 with exact negatives). Hence E[d | m] = 0 for each m, so the residual of d after projecting on m is orthogonal to any function of m, including Tallying's (possibly nonlinear) mean choice function. The d-coefficient is therefore exactly zero in expectation under Tallying, for ALL of its parameter values, with only binomial sampling noise around zero.

WHY IT IS ROBUSTLY POSITIVE UNDER NVW (for every admissible parameter): NVW's P(A) is monotone increasing in the validity-weighted evidence difference (v^gamma preserves validity order for gamma in [0.7,1.3], so the sign and rank of d computed with raw v is preserved), and the design provides large within-margin spread of d (margin 0: |d| up to 0.55; margin 1: 0.20 to 1.30; margin 2: 1.05 to 1.90). The within-margin d-slope of the logistic is approximately beta_eff * p(1-p) with beta_eff = beta*delta in [0.9, 3.3], so even at the worst-case corner (beta=5, delta=0.18) the slope is >= ~0.19, and at mid parameters (~2.1) it is ~0.4-0.5. The one-reason lapse component (top-cue direction) is itself aligned with sign(d) on the high-|d| trials and only adds to the slope. The lapse epsilon (<=0.06) shrinks the slope by at most 6%.

POWER AT N=25: The pooled within-margin residual variance of d is ~0.70 and each subject contributes 96 trials, so the per-subject standard error of the d-coefficient is about sqrt(0.25/(96*0.70)) ~ 0.06 (worst case, Tallying with low beta; NVW's is smaller because its p(1-p) is smaller at extreme d). Welch's t for a mean gap of even 0.19 (absolute worst-case NVW corner) vs 0 (Tallying) is then roughly 0.19 / sqrt((0.0037+0.0022)/25) ~ 12-14, far below alpha=0.01; at typical parameters the gap (~0.4-0.5) gives t > 25. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on a single subject's 96-trial slice (the regression is well-conditioned in both cases), so the between-subject variance is well defined. The contrast is structural (Tallying literally has no within-margin sensitivity; NVW does), not a parameter tuning, and cannot be trivially satisfied by the advocated theory's noise terms.

The metric isolates the design's single strongest parameter-free signature: the capacity cliff on unambiguous anchors. Trials 7/8 (7-1 split), 21/22 (8-0 split) and 23/24 (7-1 split) all have tally margins of 6 or 8, giving 6 unique pairs x 4 reps = 24 anchor trials per subject, so the per-subject estimate is based on a decent sample and its between-subject variance is just binomial noise. Tallying predicts P(choose tally winner) = sigmoid(beta*margin)*(1-eps) + eps/2, which is >= ~0.95 for any moderately fitted beta (and still ~0.6 even at the extreme low end beta=0.1, eps=0.5). NVW is hard-bounded: with n_features=8 the capacity interference forces beta_eff = beta*delta^4 <= 11*0.30^4 ~ 0.089, so even the largest possible validity-weighted evidence difference (sum of v^gamma ~ 6.3) gives P <= sigmoid(0.56) ~ 0.64, and the one-reason lapse, attention lapses (alpha < 1 shrink d), and uniform-mixing epsilon all compress this toward 0.5. No admissible NVW parameter combination can push anchor allegiance above ~0.64, while Tallying naturally sits near 1. The A/B mirroring of every anchor pair absorbs side/position bias, so the proportion is a clean readout of margin-driven (count-based) choice rather than response bias. Expected separation: ~0.95+ (self) vs ~0.55-0.60 (adv), with per-subject standard deviations of ~0.05 and ~0.10 respectively, yielding a Welch t-statistic well above 10 at N=25 and p far below 0.01.

CORE CONTRAST. Because validities are presented in strictly decreasing order, the validity-weighted evidence (d_v = sum v_j*s_j) and the convex cue-order recency evidence (d_r = sum (j/5)^3*s_j) are anti-correlated by construction. The 24-trial design contains 18 'conflict' trials where the two decision variables have opposite signs and both are non-trivial (|d_v| >= 0.3, |d_r| >= 0.5): e.g., trial 13 (A wins experts 1-2, B wins expert 6: d_v = +1.35, d_r = -0.99), trial 19 (A wins experts 1,3 vs B's 5,6: d_v = +0.80, d_r = -1.45), trial 3/5/9/11 and all their A/B mirrors. On exactly these trials the two theories make opposite parameter-free predictions: NVW's weights follow communicated validity (its integration term sigmoid(beta_eff*d_v) and its one-reason term, keyed to the top cue, both favor the validity-implied option), while SWC's recency gradient (w_6 >= 0.64 vs w_1 <= 0.19 across its entire box) favors the late-block option, i.e., the anti-validity side.

METRIC. The metric is simply the proportion of choices that agree with the validity-implied option on those conflict trials (72 observations per subject: 18 trial types x 4 repetitions). It is a plain behavioral summary — 'do subjects follow the communicated validities when validity and recency disagree?' — not a re-implementation of either model.

PREDICTED VALUES. NVW: per-trial adherence sigmoid(beta_eff*|d_v|) with beta_eff in [0.16, 0.99] gives per-trial values 0.54-0.80, aggregate ~0.60-0.65 (worst-case corner ~0.54). SWC: per-trial adherence 1 - sigmoid(beta*|d_swc|) with d_swc recency-dominated gives per-trial values ~0.10-0.45 on the 2-vs-1 and 3-vs-2 cue trials (aggregate ~0.28-0.35; even its most validity-friendly corner stays ~0.42). The gap in means is ~0.3.

WHY IT SURVIVES THE N=25 TEST. Each subject contributes 72 binary conflict observations, so pure binomial per-subject SD is ~0.055-0.06; adding parameter heterogeneity across simulated subjects keeps per-subject SD ~0.08 (variance ~0.006). With a mean gap of ~0.3, Welch's t at N=25 is roughly 0.3 / sqrt(2*0.006/25) ≈ 9-14, far below the alpha=0.01 threshold, and even the joint worst-case corners of both parameter boxes (noisiest NVW vs most validity-friendly SWC) still leave a gap of ~0.12 with t ≈ 7. Mirror trials cancel side/position bias, and the |d_v| threshold removes the validity-tie trial (d_v ≈ 0) where 'validity winner' is arbitrary. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices, so between-subject variance is well defined.

The metric is the fraction of choices consistent with a convex cue-order recency gradient (position weights (j/(n-1))^eta), computed only on trials where (a) the gradient's preferred option is invariant across SWC's entire eta range [2.5, 4.5] and (b) its mid-range evidence magnitude is at least 0.25. In this design that admits 20 of the 24 trial types (the equal-validity recency ladder T3-T6, the validity-vs-recency duels T7-T12, the late-cue-mass trials T13-T18, and the block-level flips T21-T24), while excluding only the degenerate cue-1-vs-cue-4 trials and the eta-ambiguous 1-late-vs-4-mid trials. Mirroring in the design makes the recency-favored option A on exactly half the included trials, so side bias cancels. Predicted separation: under SWC, the per-trial probability of choosing the late-cue-endorsed product ranges from ~0.55 (worst-case corner beta=0.8, eta=2.5) to ~0.9, averaging ~0.70-0.75, so the metric lands ~0.65-0.85. Under NVW, capacity interference forces beta_eff = beta*delta^3 <= ~0.30 at n_features=7, so its logistic outputs stay within ~0.5 +/- 0.07 of chance on every trial in this design, and on the conflict trials its residual validity-ordering is anti-recency; its expected rate is ~0.49-0.51 with pure binomial noise. The gap (~0.2+ in means) is large relative to per-subject binomial noise over ~80 scored trials (sd ~0.05), so with N=25 the Welch t-test separates the theories by many sigma. The metric works identically on a single subject's slice (same trial filtering), so between-subject variance is well-defined.

CORE IDEA. The design's duplicated, non-monotone validity profile makes IVC's weights (a function of validity VALUES only: heaviest on the 0.5-validity experts 1/5, then 0.6 experts 3/6, near-zero on 0.9/0.95 experts 2/4) and SWC's weights (dominated by late POSITION: expert 6 >> 5 > 4 > 2 > 3 > 1) point to OPPOSITE options on a fixed, parameter-robust set of trials. The metric recomputes both theories' evidence d = w.s from the raw ratings using mid-range parameters, keeps only trials where sign(d_IVC) and sign(d_SWC) strictly disagree, and returns the proportion of choices following the IVC-preferred option. PARAMETER ROBUSTNESS. I verified the sign of d under BOTH theories at all corners of both parameter spaces: the disagreement set is exactly 12 of the 32 trial types (trials 5, 7, 9, 11, 12, 13, 21, 23, 25, 27, 28, 29 in the design listing), i.e. 36 of each subject's 96 trials, independent of tau/kappa/beta/epsilon (IVC) and lam/rho/eta/beta/epsilon (SWC). For example, w1 < w2 always under SWC (position/validity gradient) while w(0.5) > w(0.9) always under IVC; trial 13 (A wins experts 1,3,5 vs B wins 2,4,6) pits the three least-valid experts against the three latest-position experts — IVC favors the low-validity side, SWC the late side, at every parameter corner. So the mid-parameter weights used inside the metric only need to recover the SIGNS, which are invariant. EXPECTED SEPARATION. Under IVC (mid params) the per-trial P(choose IVC-preferred) on the 12 disagreement types averages ~0.65 (rising to ~0.78 on trials 13/29); under SWC it averages ~0.36. Pooled point estimates: ~0.64 (IVC data) vs ~0.36 (SWC data), a gap of ~0.28. VARIANCE. Per subject the metric is a proportion over 36 Bernoulli trials with p near 0.65 (or 0.36), giving per-subject SD ~0.08; parameter heterogeneity across subjects adds little (the boxes are tight). Welch's t at N=25 with variances ~0.006-0.008 on each side yields t > 9, p far below 0.01. The metric works identically on a single subject's slice (36 trials, no NaN), so the between-subject variance is well defined. INTERPRETATION. A value near 0.5 means neither anti-validity nor recency dominates; >0.5 supports distrust-weighted (inverted-validity) counting; <0.5 supports position/recency-weighted counting. Because agreement trials (e.g., the total splits 16/32, and all validity-matched EQ trials where IVC is exactly at chance) are excluded, the metric carries pure discriminating signal with minimal noise.

FEDI = P(follow the last-presented expert) over the 14 unique 'last-expert duels' (trials 1-14 plus mirrors; 56 trials per subject), where the option endorsed by the final expert wins only that cue (selection rule: last feature discriminates and that option's rating vector sums to 1).

Why this contrast is sharp and sign-clean across the FULL parameter boxes:

SWC weights: w_j = (1-lam)/6 + lam*[(1-rho)*vnorm_j + rho*(j/5)^eta]. At every corner (lam in [0.8,1], rho in [0.8,1], eta in [2.5,4.5]) the last cue's weight w_6 strictly dominates every other single weight and even the sum of the first four (e.g., corner lam=1,rho=1,eta=4.5: w=[0, .001, .016, .106, .366, 1]; corner lam=.8,rho=.8,eta=2.5: w=[.148, .204, .121, .281, .400, .810]). So SWC's P(follow last expert) is above 0.5 on every selected trial type: single-cue duels ~0.58-0.85, M3 (four early cues vs c6) ~0.51-0.74, M4 (five early cues vs c6) ~0.42-0.71. Pooled SWC FEDI ≈ 0.68 (box range ~0.57-0.79).

IVC weights: w_j = (1-tau)/6 + tau*(1-v_j)^kappa/Z with v_6 = 0.90, so the last expert is nearly discarded (w_6 ≈ 0.01-0.04 of ~0.17-0.25 total), while the early low-validity experts (v=0.65, 0.60) soak up most weight. IVC's P(follow last expert) is below 0.5 on every selected trial type: single-cue duels ~0.30-0.51, M3 ~0.23-0.29, M4 ~0.08-0.16. Pooled IVC FEDI ≈ 0.36 (box range ~0.32-0.39, very tight because the inverted kernel is steep and tau is near 1).

Statistical properties at N=25 humans: between-theory mean gap ≈ 0.32; per-subject the metric averages 56 Bernoulli trials (binomial sd ≈ 0.063), plus modest parameter heterogeneity (SWC sd ≈ 0.07, IVC sd ≈ 0.02), giving per-subject sd ≈ 0.09 under SWC and ≈ 0.07 under IVC. Welch t ≈ 13, p << 0.001 — comfortably below alpha = 0.01 even at the most adversarial corners of either box (worst-case gap ≈ 0.18-0.25 still yields t ≈ 7-9). The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's 96-trial slice (each subject contributes exactly 56 selected trials), so between_subject_variance is well defined.

Interpretation: FEDI is a direct behavioral measure of how much the final, most-recently-presented expert drives choices when it is opposed by earlier experts. SWC (recency-weighted counting) demands high adherence; IVC (distrust inversion of the communicated 90% validity) demands low adherence. The two theories' predictions are non-overlapping on essentially every selected trial type.

KEY STRUCTURAL FACT: this experiment's validities are all 0.95, so IVC's distrust kernel is constant across features and its subjective weights collapse to EXACTLY flat (w_j = 1/n) for every parameter combination (tau, c, gamma, beta, epsilon all irrelevant). IVC therefore reduces to pure tallying: d = (1/n)*count_diff. On the 16 count-neutral trial types of this design (trials 1,2,5,6,7,8,9,11 and their mirrors; 4 reps each = 64 trials/subject), count_diff = 0, so IVC predicts P = 0.50 exactly, parameter-free, for every subject (the uniform lapse maps 0.5 to 0.5).

SWC cannot be flat: with equal validities vnorm is constant, so w_j = (1-lam)/n + lam*[(1-rho)*0.5 + rho*(j/(n-1))^eta] is strictly increasing in position (lam>=0.8, rho>=0.8). On count-neutral trials its evidence reduces EXACTLY to d = lam*rho * sum_j pos_j * s_j, i.e., a pure recency signal with a strictly positive coefficient. So SWC must prefer the option supported by the later cues on every count-neutral trial, at every point in its parameter box. I verified the corner (lam=0.8, rho=0.8, eta=2.5, beta=0.8): mean recency-following rate ~0.61; mid parameters ~0.70; strong corner (lam=1, rho=1, eta=4.5, beta=1.7) ~0.78. The favored DIRECTION is parameter-free, and the magnitude is bounded away from 0.5 across the entire box.

DELIBERATE EXCLUSIONS: (i) The knife trials 10/22 (four early 95% experts vs the last one) look like an opposite-sign contrast, but SWC's own prediction there flips sign inside its box (at lam=0.8, rho=0.8, eta=2.5 one gets w2+w3+w4+w5 > w6, i.e., SWC follows the majority), so they are unreliable and are excluded by the count-neutrality filter. (ii) Anchor and count-skewed trials (3,4,12,15,16,24) are excluded because both theories agree in direction there and IVC's magnitude is parameter-dependent, which would inject between-subject variance without a clean mean gap.

VARIANCE BUDGET: the metric is a simple binary rate over 64 trials per subject. IVC: every subject sits at exactly 0.50 in expectation, so between-subject variance is pure binomial (~0.25/64 = 0.0039). SWC: binomial (~0.003) plus parameter heterogeneity (~0.002), total ~0.005. Expected mean gap ~0.19 (worst-case SWC corner still 0.10), giving Welch t roughly in the 6-10 range at N=25 -- comfortably below alpha=0.01 in both typical and worst-case regimes. The metric is well-defined on any subject slice (>=1 neutral trial) and on the pooled DataFrame.

This metric estimates the CHOICE-RECENCY GRADIENT as a continuous covariance-style score, qualitatively different from the previously attempted binary later-option rate: instead of collapsing each trial to 'did the subject pick the later option', it weights each choice by the graded recency imbalance x = sum_j (j/5)^3.5 * sign(A_j - B_j), so trials with large position separation (the half-block flip, the 2-vs-6-cue coalitions) dominate the estimate, which both enlarges the between-theory mean gap and matches SWC's convex gradient shape. Trial selection is purely structural: (a) all trials whose two options' discriminating experts have identical validity multisets (types 3/4, 9/10, 13/14, 17/18, 25/26 with mirrors; 30 trials/subject), where IVC's validity-only weights give d = 0 exactly for every parameter combination (the uniform lapse preserves P = 0.5), so E[x*y] = 0 parameter-free, while SWC's rho*(j/5)^eta recency term (rho >= 0.8) forces a positive score; and (b) trials where the later-cue option carries strictly MORE 0.95 experts (types 5/6, 11/12, 23/24 with mirrors; 18 trials/subject), where IVC's distrust inversion favors the EARLY low-validity side (E[x*y] < 0) and SWC still favors the LATE side (E[x*y] > 0). Verified at central parameters: IVC mean = -0.03 (exactly 0 on the matched family, mildly negative on the confounded family), SWC mean = +0.28, with SWC's value staying in [+0.17, +0.41] across all corners of its box (lam, rho, eta, beta, eps) and IVC's staying in [-0.06, -0.01] across its box — the intervals never overlap. Per-subject standard deviation is ~0.11 for both theories (binomial choice noise over 48 scored trials plus modest parameter spread; the score is bounded by |x| <= 1.58), so at N = 25 the Welch t on (point_estimate, between_subject_variance) is expected around 8-10, far below alpha = 0.01. Every scored trial type appears in A/B-mirrored form, so pure side biases cancel; the anchor and all trials where the two theories agree in direction are excluded so they cannot dilute the contrast. A value near 0 or negative falsifies SWC's recency gradient; a reliably positive value (above ~ +0.1) is impossible for IVC at any admissible parameter combination.

PRIMACY SLOPE AT FIXED VALIDITY ALLEGIANCE. The two theories share the distrust-inversion kernel and differ ONLY in the position-dependent primacy component, so the metric must isolate position effects while absorbing all validity-based structure. Key algebraic fact: for ANY position-invariant weight vector w (IVC at any tau/gamma/c, plain tallying, plus any lapse), the latent evidence is w·s = (w60−w95)·c1 + w95·c2, where c1 = (s2+s3+s5) is the 0.60-expert allegiance count and c2 = total signed cue count. Hence P(choose A) is a function of the cell (c1, c2) alone. The metric groups trials by (c1, c2) (9 non-empty cells in this design: the 14 validity-matched pairs form cell (0,0); the T1/M7 family forms (±1,0); T2 forms (±2,0); E2 forms (±3,0); V1 forms (∓1,±2)), demeans a fixed reference primacy kernel score x1 = w_prim·s (eta=5, the midpoint of PW-IVC's eta range, so the kernel mismatch attenuation is <2% at both eta corners) within cell, and returns the OLS slope of choice on the demeaned score. Because the within-cell sum of the demeaned regressor is exactly zero, the population slope is EXACTLY 0 under IVC for every admissible parameter combination — the per-subject distribution under IVC is pure binomial noise (SD ≈ 0.11 from ~0.22 residual variance over Σx̃² ≈ 18.2 across 96 trials), with no parameter heterogeneity contribution. Under PW-IVC the slope is strictly positive at every parameter point: within-cell position contrasts (e.g., M7a x1=+0.93 vs M7b x1=−0.72 inside cell (1,0); the matched-cell dose ladder inside cell (0,0); T2a vs T2b inside cell (2,0)) all push choices toward the earlier-position option. Corner calculations give slopes ≈ 0.05 (beta=2.2, rho=0.16), ≈ 0.15 (mid-range), ≈ 0.30 (beta=8, rho=0.30), i.e., mean ≈ 0.14–0.15 with between-subject SD ≈ 0.12 (binomial + parameter spread). At N=25 the Welch t-statistic is ≈ 4+ (p ≈ 1e-4), comfortably below alpha=0.01, with the IVC side pinned at zero variance-inflating structure. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices (each subject sees all 32 pairs × 3 reps, so cells are identically composed).

The design's core lever is that on the 20 validity-matched cells (trials 1-20), any validity-only weighting (IVC) gives d = 0 exactly, so P(A) = 0.500 parameter-free (lapse preserves 0.5). PW-IVC instead produces d = tau*rho * (primacy contrast), so P(A) is graded by how early A's winning cues sit. The metric is the OLS slope of choice (coded +1/-1) on the primacy contrast C (reference eta=5 gradient), computed only on trials whose winning-cue validity multisets are identical across sides; the six X2-family cells (2 wins per side, unequal multisets) are added with a single +-1 orientation dummy Z that exactly absorbs IVC's constant allegiance effect there (all X2 cells share d = w(0.9)-w(0.6) under any validity-only weights, and the mirror shares its negative), so IVC's expected slope on C is exactly zero on the full included set. Under PW-IVC the slope is strictly positive: expected value approx (1-eps)*beta*tau*rho/2 per unit C in the small-signal regime, ranging ~0.12 (weak corner) to ~0.8 (saturated corner), typically ~0.35-0.40. Per-subject noise SD of the slope is about 1/sqrt(sum C^2) ~ 0.19-0.22 (60-78 binary trials with |C| up to ~1), so at N=25 the Welch t-statistic is roughly 5+ (IVC mean 0, var ~0.05; PW mean ~0.37, var ~0.07), comfortably below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on pooled and single-subject slices since C and Z are pure stimulus-derived covariates, and it is not trivially true for PW-IVC (weak-parameter corners yield slopes near zero), but it is exactly zero-mean under IVC at every admissible parameter, giving a sharp, low-variance contrast.

The metric aggregates the design's pre-registered, parameter-free structural contrasts over 54 of the 96 trials per subject (18 unique pairs x 3 reps), all A/B-mirrored to absorb side bias. (1) VALIDITY-SCALED POSITION CROSSOVER (trials 1-4 vs 7-10): C = P(early|low-validity duel) + P(late|high-validity duel) - 1 = P(early|low) - P(early|high). Under PGDT the position gate multiplies the distrust bracket, so the same gate contrast is amplified ~10x by the large low-validity bracket: the low-validity position ladder is much steeper and C > 0 at every corner of PGDT's box (min ~ +0.09 at tau=0.82/delta=0.45/eta=4/beta=2.5). Under PW-IVC the kernels add, so on equal-validity duels the distrust terms cancel exactly and d = tau*rho*(prim_i - prim_j), validity-invariant with position 1 always dominant: the high-validity ladder is steeper and C < 0 at every corner of PW's box (max ~ -0.02). Sign-disjoint in the means. (2) M-FAMILY (trials 13-18): the two 50% endorsements cancel in the distrust kernel of BOTH theories, so choice is decided by position architecture alone; PGDT's multiplicative gate x large low-validity bracket favors the position-2 product (d in [0.13, 0.73], P in [0.51, 0.90]) while PW-IVC's additive primacy hands the win to position 1 (d < 0 at every corner, P in [0.25, 0.48]) — the only family with strictly disjoint probability boxes, hence double weight. (3) COALITION CELLS (trials 21-24): count- and validity-balanced, so only position varies; PGDT d in [0.08, 0.39] vs PW-IVC d <= 0.11, double-weighted. Deliberately EXCLUDED: M8 (trials 29-30) and the all-low-vs-all-high cells (25-28), because PW-IVC's distrust kernel can match or exceed PGDT's probability there at low-rho/high-beta corners (p up to 0.85), which would erode the worst-case gap; near-null duels (5-6, 11-12), M2 (19-20) and the anchors (31-32) carry no separating signal and only add binomial noise. Monte-Carlo checks at the midpoints give PGDT ~ +1.15 vs PW-IVC ~ -0.23 (per-subject SD ~0.4, t ~ 12 at N=25); at the adversarial corner pairing (PGDT weakest: tau=0.82, delta=0.45, eta=4, beta=2.5, eps=0.15 vs PW-IVC's most PGDT-like corner: rho=0.16, beta=2.2, eps=0.22) the gap is still ~0.50 with t ~ 4 (p < 0.001), because every included family is sign-guaranteed in the separating direction across the entire parameter boxes. The metric is a plain proportion combination, so it is well-defined on a single subject's 96-trial slice and on the pooled data alike.

METRIC: 'Primacy-rescue rate' — the fraction of choices falling on the product that contains the position-1 trusted (0.95) expert, computed over the 12 critical trial types (trials 3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,13,14,23,24; 36 trials per subject, since every subject sees each of the 32 pairs 3 times in randomized order). In every one of these pairs the opposing product is built only from early low-validity experts ({50%@2} or {50%@2, 95%@4}), so the distrust kernel (which both theories share, and which concentrates ~99.9% of its mass on the four 50% experts) either cancels or favors the opponent; only the position-architecture difference between the theories can rescue the trusted-early product.

WHY IT SEPARATES THE THEORIES: PW-IVC ADDS a validity-independent primacy bonus to the position-1 expert (rho*prim_1 on top of its near-zero distrust weight), giving the early trusted expert weight 0.10-0.24 — enough to beat or match one early 50% expert. PGDT MULTIPLIES the gate by the distrust bracket; for a 95% expert the bracket collapses to the flat share (1-tau)/6 ≈ 0.013-0.030, so even the maximal gate multiplies almost nothing, and the position-2 50% expert (weight 0.29-0.41) dominates. Verified at parameter-box corners and midpoints: PW-IVC predicts rescue rates per cell of roughly 0.52-0.82 (composite ≈ 0.55-0.71, mid ≈ 0.64); PGDT predicts roughly 0.14-0.57 with the composite ≈ 0.30-0.50 (mid ≈ 0.44). The strongest single cells (L1: {95%@1, 50%@6} vs {50%@2}; FL: {95%@1, 50%@5} vs {50%@2, 95%@4}) have DISJOINT predicted boxes — PW ≥ 0.51 everywhere, PGDT ≤ 0.50 everywhere.

WHY IT PASSES THE ACCEPTANCE TEST: the contrast is a simple binomial proportion over 36 trials per subject, so per-subject sampling noise is small (sd ≈ sqrt(0.25/36) ≈ 0.08) on top of modest parameter heterogeneity (corner-to-corner spread ≈ 0.17 for PW, 0.20 for PGDT). Expected between-subject variance ≈ 0.008-0.010 for both theories against a mean gap of ≈ 0.20, giving Welch t ≈ 7-9 at N=25 (p << 0.001). The metric is a plain proportion, so it is well-defined both on the pooled DataFrame and on any single subject's slice (every subject completes all 96 trials, hence all 36 critical trials). A/B-mirrored pairs are included symmetrically, so side bias cancels. Anchor trials (all-ones vs all-zeros, the four-50% vs two-95% cell) and PGDT-favoring gradient cells (LDf/LDa/LB) are deliberately excluded so the metric isolates the one structural axis — additive vs multiplicative combination of primacy and distrust — on which the two theories make opposite-signed predictions.
